concepts.name: Presence in the readout versus causal role
concepts.summary: A J-lens readout can name a concept at a position where that concept is not driving the model's behaviour. The language-passage experiment separates the two.
concepts.explanation: In the language-passage battery the word Spanish appears among the top J-lens readouts at comparable rates under all four task conditions, including the two automatic ones. The swap test then shows that only explicit report and flexible computation follow the swapped-in value, so the readout's presence under continuation and anomaly detection is not evidence that the model is using it there. The paper draws the general conclusion that the same underlying information is available and used in every condition, and what differs is whether the computation routes through the J-space. Occupancy alone therefore does not establish causal involvement; an intervention is required. The linewrap experiment supplies the complementary case, where the intermediate is absent from the readout entirely under the automatic condition.

concepts.name: Automaticity as an operational definition
concepts.summary: The paper uses "automatic" as a label for computations it finds to be J-space-independent, and flags that this matches human automaticity only partially.
concepts.explanation: The tasks that turn out not to require the J-space—text continuation, anomaly detection, one-step factual recall—are described as analogous to things a person might do without deliberate focus, and that analogy is where the word automatic comes from. The paper states that the intuition does not always work: for some tasks it is not obvious in advance which side of the line they fall on. It therefore offers J-space-independence itself as an operational definition of automaticity in a language model, while saying that this definition aligns partially but not entirely with automaticity in humans. The label is descriptive of a measured result rather than an independent property that was tested for.

concepts.name: Anomaly detection under a swapped language
concepts.summary: One of the four passage conditions splices a sentence of another language into the passage and asks whether anything is out of place. The judgment survives a swap that overwrites the surrounding language.
concepts.explanation: The spliced sentence is an intrusion only relative to the language around it, so the task depends on the passage's language just as the report tasks do. The swap exchanges the J-lens vector for Spanish with the vector for French across the question tokens, which sets the J-space representation of the surrounding language to match the language of the intruding sentence. Were the model reading the surrounding language off the J-space, the intrusion should stop registering as one. It answers "Yes" in both conditions, which the paper takes as evidence that the coherence judgment runs on a representation the swap does not reach.

concepts.name: Fallback to a generic prior under ablation
concepts.summary: On ordinary pretraining text, ablating the J-space leaves the model fluent but shifts its continuation from a context-specific inference to a generic one.
concepts.explanation: The examples given are positions where the unablated prediction depends on an abstract characterization the model assembled silently: the topic of a clinical paper, the historical setting of a quoted speech, the nationality of the botanist behind a species name, the diagnostic versus physics framing of an imaging technique. The J-lens directions ablated at those positions are often tokens related to that characterization. With them removed the model still produces a plausible continuation, but one reflecting a generic prior rather than the specific contextual inference. This is what selective disruption looks like at a single prediction: not a loss of fluency, but a loss of the content that would have made the prediction specific to the context.

concepts.name: Exempting the model's own top tokens from ablation
concepts.summary: The J-space ablation skips any token appearing in the top ten of a clean forward pass, so that it targets internal reasoning rather than the model's intention to report.
concepts.explanation: The ablation zeroes the residual stream's projection onto the ten most strongly activated J-lens vectors at each position, across a band of layers. A J-lens vector is a direction that disposes the model toward saying its token, so ablating one for a token the model was about to output would suppress that output directly, confounding a loss of capability with a loss of report. The procedure therefore leaves untouched any vector whose token is among the top ten predictions of the unablated pass at that position. The deficits that remain are read as the J-space's contribution to internal reasoning rather than to producing the answer.

concepts.name: Item selection for the naming and avoidance test
concepts.summary: The experiment keeps only the 63 items on which the unablated model both names the implied concept correctly and avoids it correctly.
concepts.explanation: An item is retained when the model produces the implied concept with probability at least 0.85 under the naming question and at most 0.15 under the avoidance question. The filter ensures that a failure observed after ablation is a change the ablation caused, rather than an item the model was already getting wrong. It also fixes the baseline against which the effect is measured: the avoidance failure rate that early-layer ablation raises roughly fivefold starts from a low value by construction. Results are reported as per-item rates with 95% intervals over the 63 items.

concepts.name: Automatic behaviour as a limit on J-space monitoring
concepts.summary: Because automatic computations do not route through the J-space, a misaligned behaviour that has become a fixed circuit could run without appearing in a J-lens readout.
concepts.explanation: The auditing case studies find strategic and situational assessments in the J-space that the model's output does not reveal, which is what makes the lens useful for monitoring. The paper declines the stronger claim that monitoring the J-space is sufficient. It points at its own selectivity result: sufficiently automatic, well-practiced computations proceed without engaging the J-space, and a misaligned behaviour reinforced enough to become a fixed circuit might do likewise. The single-token vocabulary limit is named as a second route by which a plan could evade the readout, since a plan whose key concept has no single-token name may not surface cleanly. The lens is presented as an addition to the auditing toolkit rather than a complete one.

concepts.name: How far the flexible/automatic criterion has been tested
concepts.summary: The paper states that it cannot predict, for an arbitrary computation, whether that computation will engage the J-space.
concepts.explanation: The criterion—the J-space is engaged when an intermediate must be handed to an arbitrary, context-specified downstream circuit, and bypassed when the computation is automatic—was read off the tasks in these experiments. Those tasks were chosen because the flexible/automatic distinction is clear for them, and the paper says so. For many tasks of practical interest the distinction is not clear, and no method is offered for deciding in advance which side a new task falls on. The paper names two things a fuller account would have to do: supply such a predictive criterion, or replace the flexible/automatic distinction with something more precise.

concepts.name: The unidentified mechanism that admits content
concepts.summary: The same information enters the J-space or not depending on what the model is asked to do, which the paper reads as some analog of attentional selection without identifying the mechanism.
concepts.explanation: The character-count experiment shows an intermediate that is absent from the J-space under the linewrap instruction and present under a question requiring computation with it, on identical passage tokens. Something therefore decides what is admitted, and it responds to the task rather than to the input alone. The paper calls this an analog of attentional selection and states that it has not identified the underlying mechanism. Its contribution is a characterization of what the J-space contains and which computations depend on it; how those contents arrive is left for further work.
